title: 从开源社区到开源评价学
title_zh: 作者自序 · 中文原文
heading: 从开源社区到开源评价学
text: 我开始使用开源软件，远早于我开始理解开源社区。本科时，Linux、Apache、Tomcat 就已经出现在我的学习和实践中。那时，我最直接的感受是这些软件好用、开放，遇到问题可以查文档、读代码。至于谁在维护它们，陌生人如何合作，一个项目为什么能够延续多年，我还没有认真想过。 2017年的中国开源年会，让这些熟悉的软件名字有了另一层意义。我第一次真正接触到项目背后的人和社区。有人写代码，有人组织协作，有人帮助新人，也有人长期承担很少被外界注意的维护工作。开源开始从一组软件名称，变成我能够感受到的人与人之间的联系。后来回望，这次相遇是我走向开源研究的一个重要起点。 此后，由于个人原因，我调整了工作，来到华东师范大学数据科学与工程学院。新的环境也带来了一个很实际的问题：在一个数据学院里，怎样开展开源教学和科研？兴趣需要找到可以长期投入的方向，社区中的观察也需要转化为能够研究、能够验证的问题。我逐渐意识到，开源协作留下的大量公开记录，恰好为数据科学提供了一个丰富而真实的研究场景。 赵生宇的加入，是这段探索中很重要的一步。我们相识于开源社区。他从阿里巴巴开源办公室离开，得知我正在组建开源研究团队，便来到我这里攻读博士。我们有共同的兴趣，也带着不同的经验：社区实践让研究问题有了来处，学术训练则要求我们把问题说清楚，把证据做扎实。团队就这样一点点组织起来。 2020年，我们发布了《GitHub 2019 数字年报》。围绕2019年约5.46亿条 GitHub 公开事件日志，我们尝试描绘开发者、项目和组织的活动，也观察中国开源参与者在全球协作中的位置。对我们而言，这是第一次比较系统地用数据呈现开源生态。报告获得的关注和肯定，给了这个年轻团队很大的鼓励，也让我们看到，社区和产业确实需要这样的观察能力。同年，生宇还发表了《开源点亮未来》一文。“开源点亮未来”也由此成为我们实验室一直沿用的口号。 随着报告传播，我们也开始考虑，怎样把一次分析积累下来的能力保留下来。数据怎样采集和整理，指标怎样定义，计算过程怎样复现，结果怎样持续更新，这些工作都值得开放出来。我们将制作报告的过程与方法逐步整理成一个开源项目，这便是 OpenDigger 的由来。从一份报告走向可以共同维护的数据基础设施，我们对开源世界的研究也有了能够持续生长的依托。 2021年，OpenDigger 进入中国电子技术标准化研究院推动的木兰开源社区孵化，随后逐步为国家有关部门和机构提供开源数据服务。它的使用场景也不断扩大，陆续支持了开源社的《中国开源年度报告》、思否的《中国开源码力榜》、中国开源软件推进联盟的《中国开源发展蓝皮书》，以及 InfoQ 的开源发展研究分析。每一次合作，都使我们更具体地理解：不同使用者需要的证据，并不完全相同。 围绕 OpenDigger，我们与合作伙伴逐渐建设起一组生态项目：OpenLeaderboard 帮助人们浏览和比较，HyperCRX 把数据带到日常使用的代码托管界面，OpenGalaxy 让协作关系有了直观的空间形态；与开放原子开源基金会共建的 OpenSODA 大赛、与蚂蚁共建的 OSGraph、与湖北大学共建的 OpenTalent，则把这些能力带入数据创新、关系探索和人才培养等场景。许多新的研究问题，正是从这些具体使用中长出来的。 工具越是被使用，我们就越不能回避指标背后的问题。一个人做了多少事，与这些事产生了怎样的影响，究竟是什么关系？某个项目的活跃度下降，应当怎样理解？一个排名能够帮助谁，又可能遗漏谁？这些问题很难单靠增加数据量来回答。活跃度研究、OpenRank 算法家族和后续实证工作，使我们不断向前推进，也不断提醒我们审视测量的含义和边界。 也正是在这样的探索中，我与詹剑锋教授的交流逐渐深入。我们最早相识于他发起的 BenchCouncil 系列活动。2022年11月，我们举办了首届国际开源软件生态基准论坛，此后每年都深入参与 Bench 大会。开源研究中的数据、指标和应用问题，在这里与基准、测量和评价方法的讨论交汇起来。 詹教授对评价学的探索，让我重新审视我们已经做过的工作。过去，我们往往从一项数据或一个应用出发，寻找合适的方法；评价学则促使我们进一步说明，评价的对象是什么，在什么条件下比较，关注谁所受到的影响，又依据什么作出价值判断。那些分散在算法、平台和案例中的问题，开始有了可以贯通起来的理论线索。 2024年12月，在广州举行的 Bench 大会上，我作了关于开源评价学的主题报告，华东师范大学也获授首个国际（开源）评价科学与工程研究中心。对我们而言，这是多年实践与评价学理论进一步结合的一个节点。开源评价学由此有了更明确的研究定位：以评价学为理论基础，系统研究开放协作中的贡献、影响、价值及其评价方法。 我尤其看重其中的双向关系。理论帮助我们发现原先没有说清楚的假设，实践则让我们知道，哪些概念需要细化，哪些方法需要修正。比如，社区中长期的维护和协调工作，是否在指标中得到恰当体现；同一套评价用于不同组织时，结果还能否作相同解释；评价公布后，人们的行为又会发生怎样的变化。把这些问题带回理论，才有可能让领域研究与基础研究相互促进。 2025年 Bench 大会前后，《Evaluatology: The Science of Uncovering the Effects》英文专著正式发布，中文版也于近期面世。在詹教授的持续推动下，我看到 BenchCouncil 从会议交流逐步发展出期刊、专著、基准平台等相互支撑的学术生态。一个方向要走得长远，需要有人提出问题，也需要可以积累知识、讨论分歧和检验方法的共同空间。这给了我们很大的启发。 这本《开源评价学：理论、方法与实证》，就是在这样的背景下逐步成形的。写作使我们重新整理多年的论文、博士学位论文、工具和应用案例，也要求我们回答一个更难的问题：它们为什么属于同一个研究方向？从理论基础到测量方法，从实证研究到智库应用与学科建设，全书四个部分尝试给出连贯的回答。我们希望读者既能理解一项方法怎样工作，也能判断它适合回答什么问题。 从实践中总结理论，是一项需要克制的工作。我们自己的案例可以提供证据，却不能替所有开源社区发言；某项算法在已有数据上的有效性，也不能自动延伸为对一切情境的解释。写这本书，是为了把依据、方法和局限交代得更清楚，让后来者能够继续检验和推进。开源评价学的体系，需要在这样的积累中逐步站稳。 共同完成本书的，除了生宇，还有我的两位博士生韩凡宇和夏小雅。小雅已经博士毕业，进入蚂蚁开源办公室工作，继续活跃在国际开源社区中；凡宇也预计于2027年完成博士学业。从社区相识，到共同研究，再到把长期积累写成一本书，这几位年轻人的成长始终与团队的发展交织在一起。能够与他们共同署名，是我作为老师很珍惜的一件事。 当然，书上四个作者的名字，远不能代表全部参与者。实验室同学对数据、代码、实验和文稿的投入，学院同事的支持，业界伙伴与社区同仁提供的问题、反馈和合作机会，都是这项工作得以延续的条件。很多贡献并没有署名在封面上，却实实在在地留在了书中。谨在这里向所有同行者致谢。 回望这些年，开源也帮助我回答了刚到数据学院时的那个问题。真实场景提出需求，应用推动方法创新，创新再回到场景中接受检验，并支持更长远的发展。“场景驱动应用、应用驱动创新、创新驱动发展”，在开源研究中有了具体的内容：一份报告可以催生一个数据项目，一个工具可以进入课程和社区，一个实践中的疑问又可以成为新的研究课题。教学、科研与服务因此有了相互连接的路径。 我们由此为开发者、企业、社区、基金会和政府机构提供了数据与评价服务，也在这个过程中培养了约三十位青年人才。他们走向不同的岗位，有人继续做研究，有人进入产业与社区。对一个大学实验室来说，能够留下可被使用的成果，也能够培养愿意参与公共协作的人，是很实在的收获。 这些探索也发生在中国开源不断发展的背景下。开源已经写入“十四五”和“十五五”规划纲要，从支持开源社区到推进开源体系建设，其公共意义日益清晰。以 DeepSeek（深度求索）等为代表的开放实践，又让更多人看到，中国的技术团队可以通过分享成果，吸引全球开发者参与，建立跨越地域的合作联系。作为研究者，我们有机会参与其中，也有责任帮助人们更准确地理解这些变化。 2026年7月9日，在瑞士日内瓦举行的“人工智能向善”（AI for Good）全球峰会边会上，我代表中国科协联合国咨商开源创新专委会（CCOSI），参与发布《2026全球开源发展报告》（预览版）。报告引起的关注与交流，让我感受到，开源数据研究已经可以服务于更广泛的国际对话。从2019年 GitHub 数据的整理，到面向全球开源发展的报告，研究的范围在扩大，最初想要理解协作的愿望一直没有变。 全球对话也让评价的责任更加具体。不同地区的参与条件不同，不同社区留下的数据也不一样。一个看似整齐的比较，可能掩盖重要的差异。我们希望科学的评价能够帮助人们理解贡献、识别需要支持的地方，并为合作提供可信的依据。让开放成果更容易被使用，让长期维护和公共贡献得到更恰当的认识，是这项研究值得继续做下去的理由。 今天，人工智能的发展使这些问题更加迫切。更多人能够获得技术，并不意味着每个人都拥有同样的参与机会。如何让不同背景的开发者进入协作，如何让有价值的公共成果得到持续支持，如何让技术进步惠及更广泛的人群，仍然需要长期工作。我期待开源评价学能在其中贡献一种扎实的研究方式，使关于开放与普惠的愿望，有可以讨论、可以检验、可以改进的依据。 这本书面向国际读者，以英文写作。我仍想用中文留下这段缘起，并附上英文译文。中文是我们几位作者共同的母语，也承载着我们理解世界、交流想法和表达感谢的许多细节。保留它，是希望读者在概念、模型和图表之外，也能看见这项工作从什么地方出发，与哪些人相遇，又为什么坚持到了今天。 从最初使用开源软件，到走进社区，再到与同行共同探索开源评价学，一路走来，最重要的始终是人与人的相遇，以及由此生长出的共同工作。愿这本书成为其中的一份贡献。也愿更多读者从这里接着往前走，让开放协作的价值被更好地理解，让愿意参与的人得到更多机会，让我们共同依赖的开源生态继续生长。 王伟 2026年11月，上海

title: From Open Source Communities to Open Source Evaluatology
title_zh: 作者自序 · 英文译文
heading: From Open Source Communities to Open Source Evaluatology
text: I began using open source software long before I began to understand open source communities. As an undergraduate, I was already using Linux, Apache, and Tomcat in my studies and practical work. What struck me then was their usefulness and openness: when I encountered a problem, I could consult the documentation or read the code. I had not yet thought seriously about who maintained these systems, how strangers managed to work together, or what enabled a project to endure. The China Open Source Conference in 2017 gave those familiar software names another meaning. For the first time, I came into real contact with the people and communities behind the projects. Some wrote code; others organized collaboration, helped newcomers, or carried out maintenance that received little attention beyond the community. Open source began to take shape for me as a network of human relationships. Looking back, that encounter was an important starting point for my research. Later, a change in my personal circumstances led me to move to the School of Data Science and Engineering at East China Normal University. The new setting brought a practical question: how should we teach and study open source within a school of data science? An interest had to become a direction worth sustained effort, and observations made in communities had to become questions we could investigate and test. I gradually came to see the public records of open collaboration as a rich, real setting for data science. Shengyu Zhao’s arrival was an important step in this exploration. We had met through the open source community. After leaving Alibaba’s Open Source Office, he learned that I was forming an open source research team and came to pursue his doctorate under my supervision. We shared an interest and brought different experiences. Community practice gave our questions a starting point, while academic research required us to formulate them clearly and establish sound evidence. The team took shape gradually. In 2020, we released the GitHub 2019 Digital Annual Report. Working with approximately 546 million public GitHub event records from 2019, we examined the activities of developers, projects, and organizations, including the place of Chinese participants in global collaboration. This was our first systematic attempt to describe the open source ecosystem through data. The attention and positive response encouraged our young team and showed us that communities and industry had a real need for this kind of observation. In the same year, Shengyu published a blog post titled “Open Source Lights Up the Future.” Its title became our laboratory’s enduring motto. As the report circulated, we began to consider how to preserve the capabilities developed through that analysis. Data collection and preparation, metric definitions, reproducible computation, and continuing updates were all worth making openly available. We gradually organized the report’s processes and methods into an open source project. This was the origin of OpenDigger. Moving from a single report toward data infrastructure that others could help maintain gave our research a basis for continued growth. In 2021, OpenDigger entered incubation in the Mulan open source community, supported by the China Electronics Standardization Institute. It subsequently began providing open source data services to national departments and institutions. Its applications expanded to support Kaiyuanshe’s China Open Source Annual Report, SegmentFault’s Hacking Force China rankings, the China Open Source Development Blue Book led by the China Open Source Software Promotion Union, and InfoQ’s research on open source development. Each collaboration helped us understand more precisely how the evidence required by one user could differ from that needed by another. Together with our partners, we gradually developed an ecosystem around OpenDigger. OpenLeaderboard supported browsing and comparison; HyperCRX brought data into the code-hosting interfaces people used every day; and OpenGalaxy gave collaboration networks a spatial form that could be explored visually. The OpenSODA competition, developed with the OpenAtom Foundation, OSGraph with Ant, and OpenTalent with Hubei University brought these capabilities into data innovation, relationship exploration, and talent development. Many new research questions grew out of these concrete uses. The more our tools were used, the harder it became to avoid the questions behind their metrics. How does the amount of work a person performs relate to its effects? How should a decline in a project’s activity be interpreted? Whom can a ranking help, and whom might it overlook? More data alone cannot readily answer these questions. Our activity studies, the OpenRank family of algorithms, and subsequent empirical work moved us forward while repeatedly requiring us to examine what our measures meant and where their limits lay. During this period of exploration, my exchanges with Professor Jianfeng Zhan deepened. We had first met through the BenchCouncil activities he initiated. In November 2022, we held the first International Forum on Open Source Software Ecosystem Benchmarking, and we have participated closely in the Bench conference each year since. Questions about data, metrics, and applications in open source came into conversation there with research on benchmarks, measurement, and evaluation methods. Professor Zhan’s work on Evaluatology prompted me to reconsider what we had already done. We had often started with a dataset or an application and sought an appropriate method. Evaluatology pressed us to make further questions explicit: what is being evaluated, under what conditions is a comparison made, whose experience of the effects matters, and on what basis is value judged? Questions dispersed across algorithms, platforms, and cases began to acquire a connecting theoretical thread. At the Bench conference in Guangzhou in December 2024, I delivered a keynote on Open Source Evaluatology, and ECNU received the designation of the first International Research Center for (Open Source) Evaluation Science and Engineering. For us, this marked a further connection between years of practice and the theory of Evaluatology. Open Source Evaluatology acquired a clearer research identity: a domain grounded in Evaluatology that systematically investigates contribution, influence, value, and their evaluation in open collaboration. I particularly value the two-way relationship. Theory helps us identify assumptions that we had left implicit; practice shows us which concepts need refinement and which methods need revision. Does a metric adequately represent sustained maintenance and coordination? Can the same interpretation be retained when an evaluation is used in different organizations? How might people change their behavior after an evaluation is published? Bringing such questions back to theory creates opportunities for domain research and foundational inquiry to advance together. Around the time of Bench 2025, the English monograph Evaluatology: The Science of Uncovering the Effects was released; a Chinese edition has appeared more recently. Through Professor Zhan’s sustained efforts, I have seen BenchCouncil grow from a venue for conference exchange into an academic ecosystem supported by journals, monographs, and benchmark platforms. A field needs people who pose questions, and it also needs shared settings in which knowledge can accumulate, disagreements can be discussed, and methods can be tested. This development has been an important source of inspiration for us. Open Source Evaluatology: Theory, Methods, and Empirical Studies took shape in this setting. Writing it required us to revisit years of papers, doctoral dissertations, tools, and applications. It also required an answer to a harder question: why do these achievements belong to a single research field? Across four parts, from theoretical foundations and measurement methods to empirical studies, think-tank applications, and disciplinary development, the book attempts a coherent answer. We want readers to understand how a method works and to judge which questions it is suited to answering. Developing theory from practice requires restraint. Our cases can provide evidence, but they cannot speak for every open source community. An algorithm’s performance on the data available to us does not automatically establish its explanatory power in every setting. We have written this book to make the evidence, methods, and limitations clearer, so that others can examine and extend the work. This is how we hope the foundations of Open Source Evaluatology will become stronger. My coauthors are Shengyu Zhao and two other doctoral students of mine, Fanyu Han and Xiaoya Xia. Xiaoya has completed her doctorate and joined Ant’s Open Source Office, continuing her active engagement in international open source communities. Fanyu is expected to complete his doctorate in 2027. From encounters in the community to shared research and the writing of this book, their growth has been intertwined with that of the team. Being able to share authorship with them is something I deeply value as a teacher. The four names on the cover cannot represent everyone who has contributed. Students’ work on data, code, experiments, and manuscripts; support from colleagues in the school; and the questions, feedback, and opportunities offered by industry partners and community members have all made this sustained effort possible. Many contributions have no name on the cover but remain present in the book. I offer my sincere thanks to everyone who has accompanied us. Looking back, open source has also helped me answer the question I faced on arriving at a school of data science. Real settings generate needs; applications drive methodological innovation; and innovations return to those settings to be tested and to support further development. The principle that “scenarios drive applications, applications drive innovation, and innovation drives development” has acquired concrete meaning in our work. A report can give rise to a data project, a tool can enter a course or a community, and a question from practice can become a research topic. Teaching, research, and service have found ways to connect. Through this work, we have provided data and evaluation services to developers, companies, communities, foundations, and government institutions, while helping to educate around thirty young professionals. They have taken different paths, continuing in research or moving into industry and community work. For a university laboratory, producing work that others can use and educating people willing to contribute to shared endeavors are tangible achievements. Our work has unfolded alongside the development of open source in China. Open source is included in both the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Five-Year Plans, with attention extending from support for communities to the development of an open source ecosystem. Its public significance has become increasingly clear. Open releases by teams such as DeepSeek have also shown how Chinese technology teams can share their work, attract participation from developers worldwide, and build relationships across geographical boundaries. As researchers, we have an opportunity to take part and a responsibility to help make these changes better understood. On 9 July 2026, at a side event of the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, Switzerland, I represented the CAST UN Consultative Committee on Open Source and Innovation (CCOSI) in the release of the 2026 Global Open Source Development Report, Preview Edition. The interest and discussion around the report brought home to me how open source data research could serve a broader international conversation. From analyzing GitHub data for 2019 to preparing a report on global open source development, the scope of our research has expanded. The original wish to understand collaboration has remained. International dialogue also makes the responsibilities of evaluation more concrete. Conditions of participation differ across regions, and communities leave different kinds of data. An apparently orderly comparison may conceal consequential differences. We hope that scientifically grounded evaluation can help people understand contributions, identify where support is needed, and establish a trustworthy basis for collaboration. Making open work easier to use, and improving the recognition of sustained maintenance and contributions to the public good, are reasons to continue this research. The development of artificial intelligence makes these questions more pressing. Wider access to technology does not give everyone the same opportunities to participate. Enabling developers from different backgrounds to join collaborative work, sustaining valuable public resources, and extending the benefits of technological progress all require sustained effort. I hope Open Source Evaluatology can contribute a sound way of investigating these questions, giving aspirations for openness and inclusion a basis that can be discussed, tested, and improved. This book is written in English for an international readership. I nevertheless wanted to record its origins in Chinese and provide an English translation. Chinese is the mother tongue of all four authors. It carries many of the details through which we understand the world, exchange ideas, and express gratitude. Keeping the original is a way of allowing readers to see, alongside the concepts, models, and figures, where this work began, whom we encountered, and why we have continued. From first using open source software to joining its communities and exploring Open Source Evaluatology with colleagues, what has mattered most has been meeting people and developing shared work from those encounters. I hope this book can make a contribution to that continuing effort. I also hope its readers will carry the work further: helping the value of open collaboration to be better understood, creating more opportunities for those who wish to participate, and sustaining the growth of the open source ecosystem on which we all depend. Wei WangShanghai, November 2026 ""

title: Preface
heading: Preface
text: A contribution to open source rarely ends where it is recorded. A patch may enter a library used by other projects. A careful review may prevent a failure that never appears in an issue tracker. A maintainer may help a newcomer whose most consequential work appears years later, elsewhere. These activities leave unequal traces. Their effects travel through technical dependencies and human relationships, and their value depends on who experiences them. Evaluation enters this setting whenever someone must decide what deserves recognition, adoption, attention, or support. A contributor wants their work to be understood. A maintainer must distribute limited review time. An organization needs to understand the components on which it depends. A foundation must decide where assistance can sustain a shared capability. Each question calls for evidence, but the same observation does not carry the same meaning in every decision. Open Source Evaluatology: Theory, Methods, and Empirical Studies develops a foundation for investigating these questions. We establish Open Source Evaluatology as a domain of Evaluatology, grounded in open collaboration and connected to its practice. The parent discipline supplies concepts for examining objects, conditions, references, effects, and value. Open source gives these concepts a setting in which production crosses organizational boundaries, artifacts are widely reused, and benefits and maintenance obligations may fall on different parties. The book grows out of a sustained programme of research. Activity studies made forms of participation visible and examined the distribution of collaborative work. OpenRank developed a relational account of influence and contribution. OpenDigger made observation, classification, and computation reusable. Contribution-recognition deployments brought evaluation into community practice, where its consequences could themselves be studied. Two doctoral dissertations provide much of the extended theoretical, technical, and empirical work behind these contributions. Our position paper connected this programme to Evaluatology; this monograph develops that connection into a systematic account. The task is to explain how these achievements belong together. A descriptive measure needs an account of what it represents. A relational model needs a reason for its graph construction. An evaluation used in a course, community, or institution needs evidence about the purposes it serves and the consequences it creates. Tool development makes these inquiries practicable, while shared benchmarks and interdisciplinary research help examine the claims that follow. The book brings these responsibilities into one field without treating them as interchangeable. Theory and practice work in both directions. Evaluatology guides the choice of object, conditions, comparison, and value. Empirical findings can require those choices to be reconsidered. Neglected coordination work changes the account of contribution. A maintained successor to an archived project changes the boundary of continuity. A public ranking can change the participation it represents. An institutional report can reveal a question that the available indicators cannot answer. Such findings contribute to theory as well as to an immediate application. The eleven chapters develop this argument in four parts. Part I, Theory , establishes the inquiry. Chapter 1 defines the domain and its foundations in Evaluatology. Chapter 2 examines collective capability, stakeholder effects, sustainability, and the consequences of evaluation. Chapter 3 turns these concepts into an evaluation-system design and relates it to completed studies. Part II, Methods , develops the means of inquiry. Chapter 4 examines Activity, from collaboration records and definitions to aggregation and empirical patterns. Chapter 5 develops OpenRank’s global and community constructions, their validation, and the interpretation of relational scores. Chapter 6 explains OpenDigger and follows scalable computation and contribution recognition into use. Experiments and deployments establish the methods’ capabilities and their limits. Part III, Empirical Studies , examines how the question changes with the setting. Chapter 7 studies contribution recognition through educational deployments. Chapter 8 investigates community sustainability through archival, maintenance, exit, transfer, and renewal. Chapter 9 examines ecosystem governance through Redis and Valkey, organizational contributions, and attribution. Together, the cases connect judgments about a person’s work, a continuing capability, and an institutional arrangement. Part IV, Applications and Disciplinary Development , connects these findings to institutions and shared research practice. Chapter 10 develops open source think-tank applications through the global development report, observatories, and OpenDipper. Chapter 11 organizes the disciplinary framework, the open tool ecosystem, OpenPerf’s benchmark comparisons, and the field’s interdisciplinary foundations. It closes with research questions about comparability, visibility, reactivity, and revision, each grounded in the preceding evidence. Three distinctions remain central throughout: recorded activity, relational influence, and stakeholder value; the evaluation of a measure and the evaluation of an arrangement that uses it; and reproducible computation and a justified interpretation. Each chapter develops its own question and references. Published results retain their populations, periods, units, and values. Current formulations guide the methodological exposition, while historical findings remain attached to the definitions that produced them. Proposed extensions are distinguished from completed studies. We write for researchers and graduate students, and for maintainers, community leaders, educators, and institutional practitioners who need to examine the basis of an evaluation. Readers entering through a method can return to its assumptions in Part I; those entering through an application can trace its evidence to Part II. Open source software is the empirical centre of the book. Other forms of open collaboration require their own examination of production, rights, and affected parties. Our aim is to make collaborative work intelligible, connect evidence to consequential choices, and learn from the consequences of those choices. The resulting foundation is intended to be used, examined, and revised. Wei Wang, Shengyu Zhao, Fanyu Han, and Xiaoya Xia November 2026

title: Book Structure
heading: Book Structure
text: Evaluatology supplies the foundation. Theory specifies the inquiry, methods construct its evidence, and empirical studies examine its use. Institutional applications and shared research practice return new requirements to this foundation. Figure P.1. Architecture of the book. Solid arrows mark the progression of the argument. Dashed arrows return empirical requirements to theory and lessons from applications and validation to methods. They indicate intellectual feedback, not estimated causal effects. title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
text: Open source collaboration makes a substantial part of software production observable. It does not make the significance of that production self-evident. A project can attract more activity while accumulating a larger maintenance burden. A widely reused component can receive little visible attention in its own repository. A contributor can improve the work of others through review, explanation, and coordination without producing the largest volume of code. Evaluation must explain which of these differences matters, under what conditions, and to whom. This chapter establishes Open Source Evaluatology as a domain of Evaluatology. The parent discipline supplies an account of objects, conditions, causes and effects, and value. Our research on Activity, OpenRank, OpenDigger, and contribution recognition supplies methods and evidence through which that account can be developed for open collaboration. The aim is a cumulative field: concepts should guide empirical inquiry, and findings should be able to change those concepts and their operational realization. The argument has three elements. An evaluation question must identify its object, affected parties, purpose, and reference. Measurements and models must be distinguished from the claims attached to their outputs. An evaluation arrangement can itself become an object of inquiry when its use changes collaboration. These elements provide the foundation for Chapter 2’s account of value and sustainability and Chapter 3’s research framework. Chapters 4–6 develop and examine the methods on which the synthesis rests.

title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: 1.1 The Evaluation Problem in Open Collaboration
text: Three problems arising from the research # The first problem is the visibility of useful work. In the OpenRank Leaderboard study, a selected maintainer’s participation consisted largely of coordination across issues and pull requests. A commit-based ordering gave a different account from the community network measure ( Zhao et al., 2024 , Section 4.1). The disagreement asks a substantive question: what contribution is the evaluation intended to recognize? More records or a more elaborate algorithm cannot answer that question without an account of the work being represented. The second problem concerns the organization of participation. Our Activity study examined who contributed, what they did, when participation occurred, and where it appeared across the collaboration landscape ( Xia et al., 2022 ). Its findings include concentrated participation, different mixes of human and automated behaviour, and temporal patterns. These are consequential observations, but their interpretation depends on the undertaking. Concentration can accompany expertise and continuity, or expose dependence on a small number of people. Distinguishing those possibilities requires evidence about responsibilities, substitutes, and the conditions of continued work. The third problem appears when evaluation is put into use. Publishing a contribution ranking can change attention and behaviour. Participants in the leaderboard deployment reported changes in how they communicated and divided their work ( Zhao et al., 2024 , Section 4.2). Such responses can alter both collaboration and the public record through which collaboration is measured. The resulting inquiry has two objects: the representation of contribution and the arrangement that uses it. Evidence about the first does not settle the consequences of the second. These problems explain the sequence of Part II. Chapter 4 establishes the observations and Activity measurements. Chapter 5 asks what a relational account adds and examines OpenRank. Chapter 6 supplies the infrastructure and follows evaluation into practice. The complete results belong there. In this chapter, the studies identify the conceptual commitments needed to understand those results and to ask further questions of them. From separate research traditions to a common question # Research on open source already offers substantial accounts of collaboration. The Apache and Mozilla cases connected participation and work organization to software outcomes; a later review distinguished inputs, processes, emergent states, and outputs ( Mockus et al., 2002 ; Crowston et al., 2012 ). Open superposition explains how independently motivated layers of work can enable subsequent contributions ( Howison and Crowston, 2014 ). These studies make clear why the significance of an action often depends on work performed by others. The pull-based development literature gives that observation a concrete workflow. Submission, discussion, integration, and rejection are different events, with different implications for an artifact and the people maintaining it ( Gousios et al., 2014 ). A submitted change can create review work without producing an accepted feature. A review can improve an artifact without adding a large volume of code. An evaluation must explain which stage it observes and which consequence it seeks to assess. Our position paper began to organize such questions through Evaluatology’s objects, conditions, and results ( Han et al., 2024 ). The present book develops that connection by retaining affected objects, reference alternatives, stakeholder purposes, and the consequences of use throughout the argument. It brings the domain framework into contact with the empirical and technical work on which the following chapters are built. The resulting field has a common problem rather than a single preferred score. It asks how evidence about open collaboration can support a stated evaluative conclusion. A descriptive inquiry, a network comparison, and a deployment study can all contribute, provided their objects and interpretations remain explicit. Their conclusions become cumulative when the conditions under which they hold can be inspected and compared.

title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: 1.2 Foundations in Evaluatology
text: A shared system of inquiry # The initial formulation of Evaluatology emphasized the science and engineering of evaluation and the dependence of results on evaluation conditions ( Zhan et al., 2024 ). The subsequent Chinese monograph develops a broader account centred on causes and effects and places Evaluatology within a proposed system of scientific inquiry ( Zhan et al., 2026 ). We adopt its conceptual organization as a theoretical foundation while distinguishing that organization from the empirical evidence and method-specific assumptions needed in a particular study. Figure 1.1 adapts the monograph’s first foundational diagram. Metrology concerns the definition, realization, and assignment of structural and behavioural quantities. Testology concerns the testing of propositions and models, as well as behavioural quantities. Inferology concerns the generation of propositions and models. Evaluatology investigates causes and effects, with the narrower activity of valuation concerned with quantities of value. Their relationship is mutually supportive: a model can guide measurement, measurements can challenge a model, and an evaluative question can determine which behaviours require testing. Figure 1.1. Four disciplines within a shared system of inquiry. English adaptation of Zhan et al. (2026) , Fig. 1.1, p. 3. Shared concepts and axioms support four mutually reinforcing disciplines. Layout and wording are condensed; arrows express conceptual relationships. For open collaboration, this arrangement clarifies the roles of familiar research activities. An operational definition of review latency is a measurement task. Checking the behaviour of a data-processing procedure is a testing task. Proposing that early review helps newcomers learn introduces a model of a relationship. Investigating whether a particular review arrangement changes subsequent participation is an evaluative task. The categories organize questions; a single empirical study may contain all four. The conceptual hierarchy in Figure 1.2 provides a second foundation. The general level supplies terms such as object, relationship, event, subject, proposition, and model. The disciplinary level gives these terms more specific roles. The methodological level introduces the assumptions and operations of particular approaches to evaluation. This hierarchy helps prevent a frequent error: moving from a general statement about causes to the conclusion that a selected statistical procedure identifies them. Figure 1.2. From a shared vocabulary to disciplines and evaluation methods. Adapted from Zhan et al. (2026) , Fig. 1.2, p. 5; Section 1.3. The nine general concepts are supplied from the accompanying text; all eight method families in the original figure are retained. Branches indicate conceptual specialization. The methods overlap and have different assumptions; the diagram assigns no common identification guarantee. The eight method families in the source diagram are retained. They are not disjoint classes or interchangeable solutions. Experimental design concerns how observations are generated; potential outcomes and structural causal models provide different formal resources for posing and identifying causal questions; instrumental variables is a method requiring particular assumptions. An object causal model is another proposed representation with its own definitions. A place in a common conceptual hierarchy does not remove these differences. The value of this hierarchy for the present book is architectural. It allows a common vocabulary to connect chapters without requiring them to use a single estimation technique. A study of review practices and a study of package dependencies can share a definition of an evaluation question while requiring different observation models, comparisons, and validation procedures. Objects, systems, and conditions # The monograph distinguishes an evaluated object (EO), affected objects (AOs), and other causally relevant objects, termed confounding objects (COs) in its framework ( Zhan et al., 2026 , Chapters 8 and 10). These are roles relative to a question. A contributor can be the evaluated object in a recognition study and an affected object in a study of a mentoring programme. A repository is an artifact and an observation site; it does not automatically delimit the community or the relevant causal system. The term CO requires care when used alongside statistical terminology. The monograph’s object category concerns other objects that can influence the affected objects. It should not be equated without further argument with a confounder in a particular causal identification model. Whether an observed variable is a confounder, mediator, or consequence of selection depends on the question and the model. Translating an object-level account into a statistical design is substantive work. The source further distinguishes a real-world system (RWS), a self-contained system (SCS), and an object causal model (OCM). An SCS is a physical experimental model containing the cause object, affected objects, and relevant objects that cannot be isolated. The evaluation condition (EC) is defined as the system remaining when the EO is removed. An OCM is a mathematical representation based on influence mechanisms among objects; it models a real-world or self-contained system and must be examined against observations or tests ( Zhan et al., 2026 , pp. 117–120). These distinctions are useful precisely because they make modelling commitments visible. A database assembled from public events is an observation product. A simulated collaboration network is a mathematical construction. Neither becomes an SCS merely by selecting a subset of repositories. In an open community, preserving the relevant mechanisms while isolating an intervention can be difficult: contributors may work across groups, reviewers may share knowledge, and changes may reach downstream users. The investigator must explain which relationships the study preserves and which it abstracts away. An object-based account also helps formulate mechanisms. A mentoring arrangement may affect a newcomer’s access to guidance; guidance may change the newcomer’s capability; the resulting work may affect a review team and eventually a release. Each relation suggests observations and possible alternatives. The framework’s role is to state those relations. Their existence and strength remain questions for the relevant evidence. Effects and value # The parent monograph defines value through the consequences, for stakeholders, of differences between the effects of an object and those of a reference object ( Zhan et al., 2026 , Chapter 11). This makes evaluation more demanding than attaching favourable labels to an activity. A change can improve one outcome and worsen another, and the parties affected need not agree on the importance of either. A maintainer may value fewer interruptions, a newcomer may value access to explanation, and a downstream organization may value predictable releases. The private–collective innovation model and research on firms’ open source strategies explain why shared artifacts can support different forms of benefit ( von Hippel and von Krogh, 2003 ; West and Gallagher, 2006 ). Our framework carries this insight into evaluation by keeping stakeholder-specific consequences explicit. The distinction between effects and value is consequently analytical rather than a separation of research from practice. Evidence about effects constrains what a value judgment can reasonably claim. Purposes and stakeholder commitments determine which effects should be investigated and how they enter a decision. Chapter 2 develops this relationship in detail. Here it supplies the basis for specifying the domain and its research questions.

title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: 1.3 Open Collaboration as an Evaluation Domain
text: A domain defined by objects and their relationships # The position paper introduced project, developer, and community dimensions and combined statistical and network perspectives ( Han et al., 2024 ). These dimensions are useful points of entry. The relevant object, however, can also be an artifact, a process, an organizational arrangement, or a relationship among several communities. Its boundary follows the evaluation question. Open Source Evaluatology is the domain of inquiry that investigates the effects of objects and arrangements in open collaboration, evaluates the value of those effects under explicit conditions and purposes, and examines the consequences of evaluation itself. A repository is a technical container and an observation site. A project organizes work on an artifact or a related set of artifacts. A community includes participants, practices, and governance whose boundaries may extend across repositories. An organization can participate in several communities, and an ecosystem connects undertakings through reuse, dependencies, shared people, and institutions. These terms identify different objects and levels; they should not become synonyms merely because a dataset offers one repository identifier per row. The evaluated object can be located at one level while its effects occur at another. A component change can affect downstream applications. An organizational funding rule can alter the availability of maintainers across projects. A public recognition arrangement can affect the allocation of contributor effort. Ecosystem health research and studies of package dependencies demonstrate why an individual project’s observations can omit relevant interdependencies ( Jansen, 2014 ; Decan et al., 2019 ). Enlarging a boundary is useful when it includes relationships required by the question, rather than simply producing a larger graph. Stakeholders and affected objects likewise have different roles. A patch may affect a library’s behaviour; a service operator experiences consequences of using that library. In a learning-oriented community, the contributor can be both an affected object, through changed capability, and a stakeholder concerned with the value of that change. An evaluation should preserve these roles even when one entity occupies several of them. An explicit specification of the question # We use the working specification 𝒬 = ⟨ O , A , C , R , T , S , P ⟩ , (1.1) where O is the evaluated object or arrangement; A identifies affected objects together with their outcome quantities; C specifies conditions; R is the reference alternative; T is the time horizon; S identifies stakeholders; and P states the purpose. This tuple is the book’s organizing notation. It makes commitments inspectable and supplies no causal identification result by itself. For a descriptive Activity inquiry, O may be the recorded participation of a declared group of projects. The reference can be another period or comparison population. The purpose may be to characterize the composition of work. Relevant affected objects and outcomes can be named without claiming that the description estimates an effect on them. For a contribution-recognition study, the evaluated object can instead be the public arrangement; contributors, maintainers, and collaborative processes become affected objects. The reference concerns an alternative arrangement, and the horizon must be long enough to observe the consequences being claimed. A mentoring example shows how the same specification supports a different design. The arrangement assigns experienced reviewers to newcomers. The affected objects include newcomers and reviewers; relevant quantities include learning, continuing participation, and effort. The reference might be the existing review process. Research on sustained participation and newcomer barriers helps specify these mechanisms and outcomes ( Fang and Neufeld, 2009 ; Steinmacher et al., 2015 ). Those findings inform the question without establishing the effect of the particular arrangement being proposed. The conditions C include governance, eligibility, workload, platform affordances, and concurrent changes. They are broader than a set of regression covariates and should be distinguished from the specific evaluation-condition construction in Section 1.2 . A data snapshot, identity rule, or algorithm version records how the question was realized. Changing such a rule can change a result even when community behaviour is unchanged. Chapter 3 makes these relationships operational through the five-component evaluation architecture. The specification also identifies where disagreement lies. Researchers may disagree about the relevant community boundary, the interpretation of an outcome, the alternative against which it should be compared, or whose consequences matter. Those disagreements require different evidence and deliberation. Recording them explicitly helps prevent an apparently precise score from concealing an unresolved evaluation question.

title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: 1.4 From Measurements to Evaluative Claims
text: What a measurement establishes # A measurement assigns a quantity under a specified procedure. The validity of a stronger interpretation depends on what that procedure represents. Software measurement research examines units, instrumentation, protocols, and populations; assessment theory examines the evidence supporting score meaning and use ( Kitchenham et al., 1995 ; Messick, 1995 ). These perspectives direct attention to the connection between a calculation and the claim it is asked to support. Activity measures recorded participation under a behaviour selection, attribution rule, period, transformation, and aggregation. A larger value establishes a difference under that specification. It does not by itself establish better software or a more sustainable division of work. The SPACE framework makes a related distinction in developer productivity: activity is one dimension within a broader account of work and experience ( Forsgren et al., 2021 ). In our setting, the intended collaborative function determines which additional evidence is needed. OpenRank assigns influence or contribution through a specified graph and propagation model. Its score depends on the represented objects, relations, priors, and comparison population. Centrality research shows why an interpretation depends on the process that network connections are assumed to represent ( Borgatti, 2005 ). A relational score can make coordination visible, but a high score is not an estimate of a person’s causal effect on every outcome of interest. Prediction and explanation impose further requirements. A procedure may anticipate an outcome without explaining its causes, or explain a relationship without predicting new observations well ( Shmueli, 2010 ). A causal claim requires a defensible account of the relevant alternative and the conditions under which its comparison identifies the effect. A value judgment then connects effects to stakeholder requirements. These distinctions allocate different responsibilities to the evidence. Table 1.1. Measurements, models, and the claims they can support. Claim Example in open collaboration Required connection Description Recorded participation increased. Population, coverage, identity, eligible events, and period. Measurement Activity represents a specified account of participation. Meaning of behaviours, attribution, units, transformation, and aggregation. Relational influence An actor receives a high OpenRank score. Graph semantics, priors, propagation assumptions, and comparison population. Prediction A procedure anticipates a later outcome. Test observations unavailable during fitting and selection; a stated target. Causal attribution A recognition arrangement changes collaboration. Actual exposure, a defensible reference, and identification assumptions. Value judgment The arrangement warrants continued support. Consequences, burdens, stakeholder requirements, and alternatives. Book synthesis. Examples state kinds of claim rather than new findings. These claims impose different evidential obligations; they are not an automatic progression from one to the next. Chapters 3–6 develop the corresponding designs, methods, and evidence. Table 1.1 does not prescribe a ladder that every study must climb. A careful description can answer an important question. A simulation can test a mathematical interpretation under a stated mechanism. An implementation comparison can establish agreement in calculation. Each becomes misleading only when its conclusion is carried beyond what the design supports. Chapter 3 develops the references and validation procedures appropriate to these different claims. A conditional account of value # Let the effect contrast on the affected objects be represented by Δ A ( O , R ∣ C , T ) . (1.2) The contrast may be a vector: changes in review delay, artifact reliability, newcomer capability, and maintainer effort need not share a unit or direction. When a causal interpretation is intended, the design must establish how the reference represents the relevant alternative. When it cannot, the result should be described as an observed comparison or association. A stakeholder-specific valuation can then be written V s ( O : R ∣ C , T , P ) = v s ( Δ A ( O , R ∣ C , T ) ; P ) . (1.3) The parent monograph defines a scalar value function from multidimensional differences in effects. Here v s is a broader assessment mapping for stakeholder s under purpose P : a scalar valuation can be supplied when justified, while an effect profile or an incomplete comparison can be retained otherwise. This extension preserves the object–effect relation without assuming that the evidence already supports a common utility scale. A simple consequence clarifies why an unconditional ranking is often unwarranted. Suppose a decision uses an explicitly chosen linear valuation after orienting all outcome dimensions so that larger values are preferred and declaring their scaling. For two alternatives, let d = Δ A ( O 1 , R ∣ C , T ) − Δ A ( O 2 , R ∣ C , T ) . With admissible weights w k ≥ 0 and ∑ k w k = 1 , the value difference is w ⊤ d . If every component of d is non-negative, the first alternative weakly dominates under this family of valuations. If d has a positive and a negative component, admissible weights concentrated on those respective components give opposite rankings. This is a deduction under the stated additive model, not an empirical law of collaboration. It identifies a practical requirement: when effects conflict, a ranking depends on the permitted valuation choices. Where stakeholder commitments restrict the weights, the appropriate test is whether w ⊤ d retains its sign over that restricted set. Where effects are uncertain, the uncertainty must be propagated as well. A ranking can be defensible, but its robustness must be demonstrated over the choices relevant to its use. This result also shows why multidimensional evidence is valuable. Retaining separate outcomes allows readers to locate a disagreement in evidence, scaling, or priorities. Chapter 2 develops this formal distinction into a stakeholder effect profile and explicit conditions for accepting an arrangement. Section 3.5 then connects those conditions to a decision under uncertainty. A single score can be useful, but it should not conceal the judgments on which its use depends. The practical consequence is to preserve the evidence at the level needed for judgment. A record of review actions, a representation of coordination, a change in release outcomes, and a stakeholder’s assessment of burden can all be relevant. Collapsing them too early can remove the information needed to understand why two evaluations disagree. Their integration should follow an explicit account of the object and its consequences.

title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: 1.5 Connecting Theory and Practice
text: A connected body of research # The methods developed in this book address complementary parts of the same evaluation problem. Activity makes several forms of participation measurable within a common behavioural account ( Xia et al., 2022 ). OpenRank represents collaboration through typed relationships, allowing the allocation of influence or contribution to depend on surrounding work ( Han et al., 2026a ). OpenDigger supplies repeatable collection, contextual classification, metric computation, and access to the resulting evidence ( Wang et al., 2026 ). The leaderboard deployment examines what happens when one such representation becomes visible in community practice ( Zhao et al., 2024 ). The two doctoral studies connect these contributions to a broader research programme. Xia’s research develops activity analysis alongside questions about project continuity and sustainability; Zhao’s research develops the data platform, relational evaluation, and their applications ( Xia, 2024 ; Zhao, 2025 ). They provide context, derivations, and empirical material that a short article cannot always accommodate. A result repeated in a dissertation and an associated paper remains one evidence chain, however. Its repeated publication is not an independent replication. This organization changes the role of theory. The object-and-effect account explains why Activity needs a population and interpretation, why OpenRank needs graph semantics and reference conditions, and why a deployment must specify the arrangement actually used. Chapter 2 gives those commitments substantive content through collective capability, stakeholder effects, and continuity. Chapter 3 turns them into research designs. Part II then supplies the calculations, experiments, and deployments through which the commitments can be examined. Practice also changes the theory. A coordination case makes work visible that a code-centred description omits. An archived repository with a maintained successor prompts a distinction between the continuity of a repository and that of a function. A move from private discussion to public channels changes the observation process. These findings do more than illustrate a general vocabulary: they identify objects, mechanisms, and boundaries that the framework must represent if it is to remain useful. Evaluation becomes an object of evaluation # The leaderboard provides a particularly direct connection. In one inquiry, the object is the contribution representation: does it make relevant work visible, and do its scores admit a defensible interpretation? In another, the object is the deployed recognition arrangement: what changes when rankings, explanations, and repeated communication become part of community life? The affected objects and relevant outcomes differ across those inquiries. Visible platform activity already supports social inferences and coordination; contribution acceptance is associated with social as well as technical information ( Dabbish et al., 2012 ; Tsay et al., 2014 ). Deliberately publishing a recognition result can become another part of that setting. Campbell’s account of consequential indicators explains why changes in behaviour and in recorded statistics should be examined together ( Campbell, 2011 ). The possibility is a research problem, not a presumption that every response to evaluation is undesirable. Evaluatology permits an evaluation approach to be assessed through its own effects on results and affected parties ( Zhan et al., 2026 , Section 8.7.4). Open collaboration gives that recursive inquiry observable forms: changes in public communication, the division of work, the allocation of attention, and the effort needed to administer recognition. Benefits and burdens can coexist. Their existence, scale, and persistence require evidence beyond an increase in the score displayed by the arrangement. Chapter 6 preserves the original deployment window, model, reported coefficients, descriptive changes, and interview findings. Chapter 3 reconstructs the completed design and explains the claims its evidence can support. The source’s calendar-time comparison does not make all concurrent changes disappear, and later additions to a recognition scheme do not describe every earlier exposure. These limits establish conditions for further inquiry while retaining the original study’s contribution. Inherited concepts, domain constructions, and open propositions # The theoretical commitments have different origins. Objects, affected objects, effects, self-contained systems, object causal models, and value derive from Evaluatology. The domain architecture and the practical research programme develop those ideas for open collaboration. The question specification 𝒬 , the explicit separation of evidential claims, and the connections among the chapters are this book’s synthesis. The empirical support is correspondingly specific. Activity studies support an account of recorded participation. OpenRank’s formal analysis establishes properties of its operator under stated assumptions; its simulations and community cases examine further interpretations. OpenDigger’s experiments examine execution, and ORL examines an evaluation arrangement in use. Together they establish a substantial basis for the field while leaving broader claims about long-term capability, stakeholder benefit, and transfer across settings open to testing. This separation helps the theory develop. When an interpretation fails, the appropriate revision may concern the selected object, the representation, the observation process, or the proposed mechanism. A computational improvement can repair one part of the inquiry while another remains unresolved. The purpose of a common framework is to make those relationships examinable and to retain what the evidence has established.

title: Foundations of Open Source Evaluatology
heading: 1.6 Research Questions and Scope
text: Questions that the evidence makes answerable # The first continuing question concerns representation: which forms of work are made visible, and which are lost, when public behaviour is turned into a measure? The Activity lineage makes changes in selection, weighting, and aggregation concrete. Answering the question requires retaining the original behaviour definitions and investigating what their transformations preserve. Historical results cannot be made comparable merely by giving them a common metric name. The second concerns relationships: when does collaboration structure add information relevant to contribution or influence? The global and community OpenRank constructions provide distinct settings for that inquiry. The graph’s objects, relation types, and priors matter to the answer. A mathematical proof of convergence establishes that a calculation behaves as claimed; independent observations are needed for stronger assertions about the work or benefit represented. The third concerns use: how does an evaluation change the undertaking to which it is applied? OpenDigger makes repeated observation and computation possible, while the ORL deployment supplies evidence about one public arrangement. Repeated data can reveal changes and help investigate explanations. Their interpretation still depends on the observation process, the reference, and the actual conditions of exposure. Three propositions make the broader programme testable. Boundary sensitivity predicts that, where downstream dependence is consequential, local participation alone will omit information relevant to continuity. A comparison can test whether adding the relevant dependencies improves the interpretation or prediction of independently observed outcomes. A larger graph without such improvement would not establish the proposed advantage. Relational complementarity predicts that typed collaboration relationships can add information beyond aggregate activity when the construct depends on who enables whose work. An ablation can hold data coverage and the task fixed while changing the representation, then examine independent outcomes and sensitivity. A stable ranking or stronger correspondence with a measure using the same inputs is insufficient by itself. Evaluation reactivity predicts that public recognition can change the composition and recording of collaboration before a detectable change in long-term capability. A study can examine exposure, rewarded and unrewarded work, public visibility, and later outcomes. Changes that precede exposure or occur similarly in a justified comparison group would require a different explanation. These are propositions for further investigation, not conclusions already established for every community. Scope of the present foundation # The empirical foundation is open source software collaboration, principally observed through public development platforms. The studies concern particular populations, periods, and operational definitions. Private work, unrecorded use, and effects on parties absent from those platforms require additional evidence. Account identities, repository boundaries, and project labels are measurement choices, not complete descriptions of people or institutions. Open models, datasets, and other collaborative artifacts create related questions, but their production processes, rights, and dependencies need separate examination. Public visibility, download availability, and permission to modify and redistribute are different conditions. Transferring a metric or framework to such a setting requires an account of what remains comparable and what changes. The present chapters provide a basis for asking that question rather than assuming the transfer has been validated. The literature used here is a focused analytical selection of foundational and directly relevant work. It supports the argument without attempting to estimate the prevalence of findings across all open source research. The main evidence comes from the connected studies developed in this book. Their shared sources and overlapping populations remain identifiable, and conceptual extensions are distinguished from reported procedures and results. The argument carried forward # Part I now proceeds from a domain foundation to substantive theory and research design. Chapter 2 explains how collaborative work creates and renews collective capability, how effects matter to stakeholders, and how continuity can extend beyond a repository. Chapter 3 connects that account to questions, populations, models, references, and evidence, using three completed designs. Part II implements and examines those designs. Chapter 4 develops Activity and its empirical account of participation. Chapter 5 establishes OpenRank’s operator, global and community constructions, and validation evidence. Chapter 6 develops OpenDigger and examines computation and deployment. Evidence is therefore present throughout the methods, rather than postponed to the application chapters. Part III extends the inquiry across contribution recognition, community continuity, and ecosystem governance. Its task is to examine transfer, additional outcomes, and differences among settings, building on the method evidence already established. The concluding synthesis returns those findings to the field’s questions. The foundation offered here is a common language for that cumulative inquiry, with the objects, evidence, assumptions, and grounds of judgment open to inspection.
